5.0.0.en: Nehemiah met a great problem among the people of God, for the poor came forward with a complaint, crying out to God and to the governor Nehemiah against the exploitation of them by the rich Jews during the economic hardships they were passing through. They were barely getting the necessary food, or less than it, and suffered from the problems of humiliation and bondage.

5.0.1.en: It is noticed that most of the Jews were poor and faced this suffering, as shown by their saying "the cry of the people," and from the severity of their misery the women went out with their husbands, so that Nehemiah would lift the injustice from them and help them to live.

5.1.0.en: The complaint of the poor contained the following:

5.1.1.en: 1- The large number of sons and daughters in poor families, and this was customary and still is to this day.

5.1.2.en: 2- Their great need for the necessary food, which is bread, so they declared that they had no wheat.

5.2.0.en: It is clear from this verse that Judea was suffering from hunger, and this was due either to the scarcity of rain or to the people's neglect of farming during the building of the wall.

5.2.1.en: The poor people were forced to give their fields, the inheritance of their fathers, in pledge to their rich brethren in order to obtain their necessary food, which was wheat.

5.2.2.en: These rich among the Jews had either brought money from Babylon and its surroundings, where they had lived before their return from the captivity, or had special activity and abilities that qualified them to set up projects and succeed in them, so they obtained much money.

5.2.3.en: The rich took their brethren's fields in pledge in order to give them the necessary food, and this was contrary to the Law, because the Law forbids exploiting the poor and seizing their possessions (Deut 24:10-13); that is, a pledge is acceptable if it is for setting up projects and not for necessary needs.

5.3.0.en: The king's tribute: taxes collected by the empire from all the peoples subject to it, so that they pay a tax on every person.

5.3.1.en: The poor people also suffered from their inability to pay the king's tribute, and they were forced to borrow from their rich brethren to pay the tribute, and these loans carried usury. This is contrary to the Law, as we said, because usury is permitted in dealings between the rich with one another, but as for the poor, the Law provides that usury is not to be taken from them (Ex 22:25, Mt 25:27).

5.4.0.en: The complaint of the poor also included their being forced to sell their daughters as maidservants to their rich brethren. This was very painful to their souls, because they were unable to free their daughters so that they might live with them in their homes a dignified life.

5.4.1.en: The complaint was severe, for the poor said that they were circumcised in their flesh like their brethren, so why should they be enslaved to them.

5.4.2.en: The strange thing is that the rich among the Jews forgot that a short time earlier they had all been enslaved to Babylon, and before it to Assyria. But when their circumstances became easier and they obtained some money, they seized the opportunity of their brethren's poverty and enslaved them in selfishness.

5.4.3.en: May you be merciful to those around you and feel their material and psychological needs, so that you obtain God's mercies on earth, and after that in heaven.

5.5.0.en: Nehemiah listened attentively to the people's complaint, which came from suffering hearts, and was not distracted from them by his concern for building the wall or by repelling the plots of the enemies. This shows Nehemiah's fatherhood and his justice as a responsible governor.

5.5.1.en: This anger of Nehemiah, the responsible one, declares the uprightness of his heart and his rejection of sin, and on the other hand reassures the wronged that he cared for them and would not neglect their demands. At the same time this anger shows Nehemiah's impartiality toward the rich: he wants nothing from anyone, and he is strong, declaring the truth even if he angers some people, even if they are among the great of the people, for he fears God and therefore fears no one. This is the first step Nehemiah took, namely his anger at sin.

5.6.0.en: The second step Nehemiah took was consulting with himself. His anger was not impulsive, but he thought wisely how the just and fitting course of action should be.

5.6.1.en: The third step: with courage he rebuked the rich and the rulers of the people for exploiting the poor and for their silence about the injustice, because they took usury when they lent to the poor, although they knew of their inability to pay for the necessities of life.

5.6.2.en: The fourth step: he set a great assembly against the exploiting great men, namely a large number of the poor people as representatives of the rest of the people; that is, he confronted the rich with what they had done to these poor, and the truth became clear, which was injustice and severe exploitation. He is just, hearing both points of view, the complainant and the one complained against, to be sure of the soundness of the case.

5.6.3.en: By these actions and what follows in the next verses Nehemiah's distinction from Ezra in the internal reform of the people appears. Ezra wept and tore his garments, declaring his distress at the evil (Ezra 9:3-5), but Nehemiah added strong steps in the reform, for he rebuked the wrongdoers and did good things, as will appear in the rest of the chapter.

5.7.0.en: Nehemiah said in his rebuke of the great men that many of the Jews had been enslaved to the Gentiles, and Nehemiah and other godly men had been able to free as many as possible of the enslaved Jews. Nehemiah wonders at the great men, that after their brethren were freed they go back and enslave them. So the great men were silent in shame and in acknowledgment of their sin.

5.8.0.en: Nehemiah showed them their sin in exploiting their poor brethren, and that this conduct of theirs was evil and angered God, and by this sin of theirs they declared their lack of fear of God and their treating evil as permissible.

5.8.1.en: On the other hand, they increase the Gentiles' reproach against them, since they are poor and humiliated, and therefore this declares the inability of their God to provide for them and give them a dignified life, and by this the rich insult God. Then the Gentiles find a clear sin in the people of God, namely their cruelty and their wronging one another; that is, that the Law of God cannot spread justice among His people.

5.9.0.en: The fifth step Nehemiah took in solving this problem was a positive action by him and those working with him in managing the affairs of Jerusalem, for they came forward to help the poor with money that they lent them to meet their needs, so that they would not need to borrow from the rich usurers who exploited them. At the end of the verse, as a sixth step, he demands of the rich that they leave off usury, that is, when they recover their money from the poor they do not take more than what they lent.

5.9.1.en: And out of Nehemiah's humility he says "let us leave off this usury," to encourage the rich to do so. He did not say to them "leave off," but "let us leave off," and this was great gentleness on his part.

5.10.0.en: The seventh step Nehemiah took was his command to the great men and the rulers to restore at once the fields and houses they had taken in pledge from the poor, and by this they would have an opportunity to find food and live a dignified life.

5.10.1.en: He also demanded that they restore the usury they had taken, the amount of which was the hundredth part, that is, 1% monthly, and this means that they were taking 12% a year as interest on their loans to the poor.

5.11.0.en: The great men obeyed Nehemiah and restored the property and money to the poor, and this shows the extent of Nehemiah's awe and authority, so that the great men feared him, for they saw in him the Spirit of God and justice.

5.11.1.en: The eighth step was Nehemiah's appointing the priests as responsible for carrying out what the rich had promised, considering the priests as knowing the Law and responsible for carrying it out, to warn every one who fell short or was slack in it. By this Nehemiah confirmed the promise of the rich, and it became a covenant between them and God, whom the priests represent.

5.12.0.en: I shook my lap: shaking the lap was an ancient custom meaning the cursing of the other person. They used to make a pocket in the garment in which they put leaves or anything similar, and they shook it out when needed to declare their curse and anger on whoever stood before them.

5.12.1.en: The ninth and last step Nehemiah took was shaking out his lap before the great men, declaring that curses would come upon everyone who did not carry out what he had commanded, that is, he would be cursed by God, deprived of every blessing, and God would shake out every person who did not do this, that is, forsake him and drive him far away and empty his house of blessing, because he had not put out of his house and his possessions the money of injustice that he had taken from the poor. The great men agreed to Nehemiah's words, saying "Amen," as the people did long ago in the days of Moses at the mountains of Gerizim and Ebal, when they heard the blessings and the curses that would come upon them for obeying God's commandments or rejecting them.

5.12.2.en: After this the great men prayed and praised God and glorified Him because He had turned them back from sin so that they might live by His commandments, and they carried out all that God commanded through the mouth of Nehemiah, and were saved from falling into division between the rich and the poor and the revolts that result from it.

5.12.3.en: If you are responsible in any place, do not be lax with sin, and declare your anger at it, so that everyone around you turns back from it. Declaring the truth is your first responsibility, so that you are the first to keep the word of God.

5.13.0.en: Nehemiah became governor of Judea by the command of King Artaxerxes, when he declared to him his concern to build a wall for Jerusalem. He remained governor for twelve years.

5.13.1.en: During this period Nehemiah was an example of sacrifice, for he did not use his natural right to obtain his material needs of food and drink, for himself and his brethren, or his helpers in administering the province, or his relatives, but gave up this right. He took no taxes from the people to provide for his needs, but it seems that he relied on his own money, which he had obtained when he worked as cupbearer to the king in the capital Shushan the palace, before he became governor of Jerusalem and Judea.

5.13.2.en: Nehemiah's giving up his natural right shows the following:

5.13.3.en: 1- That he is an example in giving and in feeling for the poor, so that the rich would imitate him, and he did not of course intend boasting. The rest of the chapter shows his noble purpose.

5.13.4.en: 2- Since he gave up his right, he is not biased in his command, but gave a lesson to the great men to keep the Law and have compassion on their poor brethren, for he does not want to take anything of the money of the rich for himself.

5.13.5.en: May you learn self-giving from Nehemiah if you are responsible in your home, or your work, or a servant in the Church, so that you prefer the comfort of others and give up your own comfort and material needs, and put others before yourself.

5.14.0.en: A shekel of silver: equal to 11.6 grams (the shekel of the sanctuary). The governors who preceded Nehemiah in governing Jerusalem and Judea were accustomed to take from the people the needs of the governor's palace of food and drink, in addition to forty shekels of silver, equal to about 464 grams, that is, about half a kilogram of silver, and this was most likely given daily to the governor's palace. They paid no heed to the poverty and weakness of the people but looked to their own comfort.

5.14.1.en: These governors are not meant to be Ezra or Zerubbabel, but the governors who were foreign to the Jews, whom the empire appointed.

5.14.2.en: We see Nehemiah's love and his keeping away from error in not condemning a certain person, in that he did not mention the names of these governors. He does not intend to condemn anyone, but to make clear the idea of self-giving that Nehemiah practices, and he calls the great men to follow it.

5.14.3.en: The burdening of the people was in three things, which are:

5.14.6.en: 3- The governor's helpers exploited the people and obtained money and possessions from them.

5.14.7.en: Because Nehemiah feared God, he refused to exploit the people, or even to obtain only his personal needs from them, because he had compassion on them. By this he is an example for the great men to fear God and not exploit the poor.

5.15.0.en: Nehemiah's goodness as governor appears in the following:

5.15.1.en: 1- His first concern was the completion of his work, which was building the wall, and not his personal comfort as governor.

5.15.2.en: 2- He did not care to own fields or any possessions, but on the contrary used his personal money to help the poor of the people.

5.15.3.en: 3- Because Nehemiah was concerned to stand in person to oversee the work of building the wall and its gates, his helpers also moved to manage the building work in imitation of him, and did not seek their own comfort by exploiting the people. From this appears the difference between Nehemiah's servants, that is, his helpers, and the servants of the former governors, who exploited the people.

5.16.0.en: Nehemiah used to host in the governor's palace more than a hundred and fifty men, who were:

5.16.1.en: 1- The Jews who came with him from Babylon.

5.16.2.en: 2- The Jewish rulers responsible for the cities subject to him.

5.16.3.en: 3- The Gentile rulers governing the cities subject to him.

5.16.4.en: 4- The guests from the Gentile nations surrounding Judea, who visited the governor.

5.16.5.en: Nehemiah spent on these daily tables from his personal salary, which he obtained as the king's governor, in addition to his money that he had and had saved when he was the king's cupbearer, but he did not exploit the people to obtain money.

5.16.6.en: Nehemiah here is a type of Christ, who offered His table, that is, the altar of the Church of the New Testament, to Christians of Jewish or Gentile origin. He offered on His table the greatest food, which is His most holy Body and Blood, as Nehemiah offered the greatest foods and wines he could.

5.17.0.en: Nehemiah shows us the hugeness of the tables in his palace: they required the slaughter of an ox daily, in addition to six choice sheep, and likewise a large number of birds, the number of which is not mentioned because of their abundance. He also offered the different kinds of wines at greater tables held every ten days in the governor's palace.

5.17.1.en: All this was at Nehemiah's personal expense, because his tender heart had compassion on the poor people, who suffered from the cruelty of bondage to the empire, for they paid it heavy taxes despite the weakness of their resources, as appears in (v. 4). From these tables we understand that Nehemiah was distinguished by the virtue of clearly welcoming strangers, as Abraham, the father of fathers, did (Gen 18).

5.18.0.en: In all that Nehemiah did of self-giving and sacrifices we see the following meanings:

5.18.1.en: 1- He offers all his good works to God, and does not intend by them any special honor or praise from anyone.

5.18.2.en: 2- In humility he declares his need to God, that he needs God's goodness and care for him.

5.18.3.en: 3- In self-emptying of his own will he did not specify particular requests from God, that is, the kind of good he wanted from God, but left that to God to choose for him the good that suits him, for he trusts in God and so does not ask for personal desires.

5.18.4.en: The completion of the wall despite the plots. The enemies of Nehemiah, who signify the demons, tried to stop the building of the wall, which signifies the building of our spiritual life, by means of:

5.18.6.en: 2- Internal wars of problems among the people of God (ch. 5).

5.18.7.en: 3- Wars directed at the leader Nehemiah to get rid of him, so that the building would stop (ch. 6).
